q: Ultrasound used in medical scanning is sound with a frequency:
o: Below 20 Hz, too low for humans to hear
Above 20 kHz, too high for humans to hear
Between 20 Hz and 20 kHz
Equal to that of visible light
x: Ultrasound means sound above the upper limit of human hearing, about 20 kHz; medical scanners use a few MHz. Below 20 Hz is infrasound, and sound is a mechanical wave, not light.

q: In an ultrasound probe, the same piezoelectric crystal acts both as the transmitter and as the receiver. It can receive because:
o: A returning echo makes the crystal vibrate, and the stressed crystal produces a potential difference
The echo heats the crystal and changes its resistance
The echo makes the crystal emit light
The crystal stores the outgoing pulse and compares it with the echo
x: An alternating p.d. makes the crystal vibrate and send out ultrasound; an echo that squeezes and stretches the crystal makes it produce an alternating p.d. (the piezoelectric effect), which the machine detects. The same effect works both ways, so one crystal does both jobs.

q: A doctor changes from 2 MHz to 8 MHz ultrasound to examine a structure. Compared with the 2 MHz waves, the 8 MHz waves give:
o: Finer detail but less penetration into the body
Coarser detail but deeper penetration
Finer detail and deeper penetration
Exactly the same image
x: A higher frequency has a shorter wavelength (λ = v/f), so smaller details can be resolved, but it is absorbed more strongly by tissue, so it does not reach as deep. That is why high frequencies are used for shallow organs and lower ones for deep organs.

q: For a PET scan, the patient is given a tracer, such as a sugar labelled with fluorine-18, that collects in active tissue. The radioactive atoms in the tracer emit:
o: Alpha particles
Neutrons
Ultrasound pulses
Positrons
x: PET means positron emission tomography: the tracer emits positrons, each of which meets an electron and annihilates into two gamma-ray photons that travel in opposite directions and are detected. Alpha emitters would be far too damaging inside the body.

q: Before an X-ray image of the stomach and intestines is taken, the patient swallows a 'barium meal'. This is done because barium:
o: Emits X-rays of its own
Absorbs X-rays strongly, so the outline of the soft gut shows clearly
Lets X-rays pass through more easily
Is a positron emitter
x: Soft tissues absorb X-rays about equally, so the gut barely shows; barium, a heavy element, absorbs X-rays strongly and acts as a contrast medium, so the parts it fills appear clearly on the image. It is not radioactive.

q: The intensity of a beam of X-rays is halved by every 2 mm of a certain material (its half-value thickness). The fraction of the intensity that passes through 6 mm of the material is:
x: 6 mm is 3 half-value thicknesses, so the intensity is halved three times: (½)³ = 1/8. Dividing by the number of thicknesses (1/3) treats the fall as linear, which is wrong for absorption.
